awd_titl_txt: Conference: Seventh International Conference on the Effects of Noise on Aquatic Life
awd_abstract_narration:
This award provides partial support for the seventh International Conference on "The Effects of Noise on Aquatic Life" to be held in Prague, Czech Republic, from June 29 to July 4, 2025. This conference builds on the success of previous meetings held in Nyborg, Denmark (2007), Cork, Ireland (2010), Budapest, Hungary (2013), Dublin, Ireland (2016), The Hague, Netherlands (2019), and Berlin, Germany (2022). The major goal of this conference is to advance the understanding of underwater noise impacts on aquatic life, with a particular focus on progress achieved since the last meeting in 2022. Support is requested primarily seeking funding primarily to support the participation of students, postdoctoral researchers, and representatives from developing nations, enabling them to attend and contribute to the meeting.

The meeting should help shape future research and understanding of effects of noise on aquatic life. Based on experience from the earlier meetings, the interactions and networking that took place has resulted in new collaborations between investigators and industry.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project investigated how hormones change the way the auditory system detects and processes sound. We used the plainfin midshipman fish, a highly vocal species in which females rely on hearing to locate calling males during the breeding season. Previous work showed that female midshipman become more sensitive to behaviorally important sounds when they are reproductively active. Our goal was to determine whether the steroid hormone estrogen drives these seasonal changes and to identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved.

Intellectual Merit: A major outcome of this project was the discovery that estrogen can directly enhance hearing sensitivity at the level of the inner ear. Females treated with physiologically relevant levels of estrogen showed auditory thresholds that were 9–15 decibels lower than those of control females, corresponding to an approximately 3- to 5.5-fold increase in sensitivity. These findings provide strong evidence that hormones can “re-tune” the peripheral auditory system and alter how sensory receptor cells respond to sound.

The project also examined how seasonal and hormonal changes affect the production, addition, and survival of sensory hair cells, the receptor cells responsible for detecting sound, and the molecular signaling pathways that may regulate these processes. We combined auditory physiology, cellular analyses, gene expression studies, and advanced imaging to investigate how estrogen acts on the inner ear. New hybridization chain reaction labeling methods and custom molecular probes allowed us to visualize the expression of specific genes in hair cells and surrounding supporting cells with much greater precision. Together, these studies provide an integrated understanding of how hormones link an animal's reproductive state to changes in sensory function.

These findings advance auditory neuroscience, sensory physiology, and neuroendocrinology by demonstrating that sensory systems are more dynamic than previously appreciated. Rather than functioning as fixed detectors of the environment, auditory receptor cells can be modified by an animal's internal hormonal state. This work also provides a broader understanding for investigating hormone-dependent changes in other sensory systems and across vertebrate species.

Broader Impacts: The project provided extensive interdisciplinary research training for graduate and undergraduate students. Students gained hands-on experience in animal care and field collection, experimental design, auditory electrophysiology, molecular biology, imaging, data analysis, and scientific communication. Collaboration among laboratories at the University of Washington and Washington State University Vancouver also gave trainees experience working in multidisciplinary research teams.

Project findings were shared with scientific and educational audiences through seminars, research meetings, conference activities, peer-reviewed publications, and public-facing science communication. Notably, the project contributed to a Frontiers for Young Minds article, “Plainfin Midshipman Fish: Songbirds of the Sea,” written to introduce young readers to fish communication and hearing.

Overall, this award advanced fundamental understanding of how hormones shape sensory perception while training the next generation of scientists and communicating the importance of basic auditory research to broader audiences.
